articles.headline: OFAC Removes Entity from Venezuela-Related Sanctions List
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a Venezuela-related designation removal on October 14, 2026. This action signifies a change in the U.S. sanctions policy concerning specific entities tied to Venezuela.

While the specific entity removed was not detailed in the initial announcement, such removals typically indicate either a change in the entity's behavior, a successful appeal, or a broader shift in diplomatic strategy. This follows previous guidance from OFAC indicating a potential snapback of sanctions on the Venezuelan oil and mining sectors if progress towards a free and competitive 2024 presidential election was not made.

The removal comes amidst ongoing international discussions regarding the effectiveness and impact of sanctions on Venezuela's political and economic landscape. The U.S. has previously used sanctions relief as a tool to encourage democratic reforms in the country.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Actions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) implemented new designations on October 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions underscore the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to disrupting illicit financial networks globally.

These designations aim to sever financial ties and restrict the resources of those engaged in drug trafficking and terrorist financing, thereby protecting the U.S. financial system from abuse. The specific individuals and entities were not immediately detailed in the announcement, but such actions typically involve asset freezes and prohibitions on transactions with U.S. persons.
This move is part of a broader strategy to combat transnational criminal organizations and terrorist groups that pose a threat to national security and international stability.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for Sanctions Violations Totaling $11.6 Million
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, for apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs. The settlement amount totals $11,662,930.

The violations occurred when Bank of America channeled correspondent banking payments through blocked banks due to technical and human error, allowed designated individuals to make payments and withdraw funds due to poor sanctions alert calibration, failed to promptly update watchlists following OFAC designations, and mishandled business accounts associated with blocked persons due to human error.

As a result of these compliance failures, Bank of America processed millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

articles.headline: OFAC Reaches Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Issues ICC and Burma-Related Actions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026, alongside new designations related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and a designation removal concerning Burma. The settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

In addition to the settlement, OFAC issued new general licenses related to the International Criminal Court, indicating specific authorized transactions or activities. Concurrently, a designation removal was announced concerning Burma, signaling a change in the sanctions status of a previously listed entity or individual.

These actions reflect OFAC's multifaceted approach to sanctions enforcement, combining civil penalties for non-compliance with targeted designations and general licenses to achieve foreign policy and national security objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. General Licenses authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs.

The specific scope of this new General License was not immediately detailed, but such issuances typically aim to facilitate certain humanitarian activities, wind-down periods for specific transactions, or other activities deemed consistent with U.S. foreign policy objectives.

This action follows a series of measures by OFAC to refine and adjust the implementation of Russia-related sanctions, often in response to evolving geopolitical circumstances and the need to mitigate unintended consequences.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Iran-Related Designations, Issues New General License, and Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026, alongside the issuance of a new Iran-related General License and an amendment to an existing Russia-related General License. These actions reflect the U.S. government's continued pressure on Iran while also adjusting measures related to Russia.

The Iran-related designations target individuals and entities deemed to be supporting the Iranian regime's illicit activities, further restricting their access to the international financial system. Concurrently, the new Iran-related General License may permit certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, potentially for humanitarian aid or other specific purposes.

The amendment to the Russia-related General License indicates a modification to previously authorized activities, which could either expand or narrow the scope of permissible transactions under the existing sanctions regime. This dynamic approach allows OFAC to respond to ongoing developments in both regions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Designations Removals and Updates, Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designations removals and updates on October 5, 2026, alongside the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). These actions signal adjustments to existing sanctions programs and enhanced guidance for compliance.

The designations removals and updates indicate a recalibration of OFAC's lists, potentially reflecting changes in the status of previously sanctioned individuals or entities. The Iran-related OFAC Alert warns that foreign financial institutions (FFIs) that continue to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions could be targeted at any time without advance notification.

The amended Iran-related FAQ 156 removes earlier language suggesting OFAC would generally contact an FFI about its conduct before making a finding of sanctionable activity, emphasizing the heightened risk for FFIs with exposure to Iranian banks.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on October 2, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in supporting terrorist organizations and their activities globally.

These actions aim to disrupt the financial networks of terrorist groups, preventing them from accessing funds and resources necessary to carry out their operations. The specific details of the designated parties were not immediately released, but such measures typically involve asset freezes and prohibitions on transactions.
The U.S. government continues to prioritize counter terrorism efforts through financial sanctions, working to safeguard the international financial system from exploitation by malign actors.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Updates Listings, and Targets Transnational Criminal Organization
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and designations updates on October 1, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC designated a transnational criminal organization and published an Iran-related Determination and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ).

These Iran-related actions are part of ongoing efforts to exert financial pressure on the Iranian regime and its affiliates, targeting various sectors and illicit activities. The designation of a transnational criminal organization highlights the intersection of sanctions policy with broader law enforcement objectives.

The Iran-related Determination and amended FAQ provide further clarity and guidance on specific aspects of the Iran sanctions program, assisting stakeholders in understanding their compliance obligations.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Removes Belarus, Narcotics, and Libya Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting counter terrorism and transnational criminal organizations on September 30, 2026. Simultaneously, OFAC issued designations removals related to Belarus, counter narcotics, and Libya.

The new designations aim to disrupt the financial networks of groups involved in terrorism and organized crime, reinforcing the U.S. commitment to combating these threats. These actions typically involve freezing assets and prohibiting transactions with the designated parties.

The removals of designations concerning Belarus, counter narcotics, and Libya indicate a recalibration of sanctions in these areas, potentially reflecting changes in geopolitical circumstances, successful compliance, or shifts in policy.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has assessed a civil penalty of $11,662,930 against Bank of America, N.A. for apparent violations of various sanctions programs.

This penalty is part of a broader enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC for anti-money laundering and sanctions compliance failures.

Bank of America admitted to willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and failed to implement and maintain an AML program that met minimum requirements, conduct due diligence for correspondent accounts for foreign financial institutions, and file Suspicious Activity Reports.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
